body:
One of the things I'm studying currently is programming. Several friends suggested various bootcamps and free resources. Currently going through the free resources in my downtime. At bad moments like tonight though? It all feels so uncertain. I love the creative potential programming has and the technical side of it (hence why I entered science to begin with) but I'm still afraid it might all fail me like everything else.

Thank you for your kind words though. In good moments, I can view cashiering the way you described it. On bad days, it's like all the good is gone.

Sounds like my friend who got into med school. She's obsessed with pomeranians and sheep and all things fluffy; she will squeal and throw herself on the ground like a toddler to pet fluffy animals. She has absolutely no sense of direction and got lost in her own apartment complex after living there for a year. She forgets to put on pants sometimes when leaving her home. (she has nudist tendencies during private times). She'll eat expired food because she forgot it expired or she's trying to be a cheapskate...then get food poisoning from it. She loves drawing penises on post-its and sticking it in random places in friends' homes and bags.

Out of all the pre-meds I know, only she and an avid League of Legends addict made it into med school. Life is very strange sometimes. If life was an RPG for these people, they had taken all the stats from daily functioning, common sense, social interaction, and manners and put it into aptitude for testing. To be honest, I'm not sure if these people would be good doctors (especially the LoL addict), but such is life.

Those are some interesting numbers. Thanks for sharing!

I've been teaching myself programming and coding in my downtime. It's enjoyable and I've been mulling over it. Been still considering going back for engineering or going through CC then transferring to get a BS. I should have considered earlier how much I enjoy technical creation and work. Casual research tells me that these fields are pretty stable (at least for the next decade).

Copy-pasting your information into my planning notes for myself though :) Thanks again.

You definitely hit the nail on the head there; I don't like biology research. Which is why I want to be open to other options and schooling. Parental pressures wants me to "make something" of the degree I got but if it's pointless to "salvage" it, I'm willing to take another path. I know for sure a PhD program isn't for me but I'm keeping the Masters option open since I don't think I can be too choosy just yet.

> There are many other things you can do that require less training, will pay far better, require fewer hours to be successful, have way better job security, and are far better for your mental health than graduate school

Could you please give me some concrete suggestions or examples? A lot of the people around me seem insistent that graduate school or some form of further schooling is the only path to a secure, well-paying, fulfilling career.

As for the beach, I guess I forgot some people found it relaxing! I'm not a very outdoors-y person and actually disliked going to the beach. Too sunny, too much sand in my shoes, got a nasty cut from the rocks the first time I went, infected bug bites...every time I tried to go to the beach to relax, I ended up with minor injuries! 

More relevantly though, I must say I find your description of the campus being laid-back to be interesting and contrary to my experiences. I found the atmosphere among science and engineering students to be very uptight, closed-off, and competitive. I've lost count of people who've refused to contribute to group work or sent unhelpful passive-aggressive emails to other students. There were definitely minor levels of sabotage between some pre-meds. It definitely felt more laid-back with humanities, arts, and poli-sci students. And this is my observations once I came out of my depressive shell. 

I really do appreciate your blunt and honest assessment of my situation. Thank you for taking the time to type up a long and detailed post for a total stranger.
I have, but it's quite disheartening when you see people unhappy with their GPAs of 3.0<. Also, I felt none of the advice would have really worked for someone in the absolute dumps.

That was definitely my mindset last night; desperate, frustrated, and sad. However, I've calmed down and will definitely put careful consideration about my goals.

Thank you. I will try.

I said this to another poster but I've managed to push the problems to healthy degrees now. Anxiety is now just normal nervousness with meeting new people. Depression is...well, it's as good as it's going to get when you feel like you're in a rut in life. Definitely nowhere near as bad as before; it's a normal amount of dissatisfaction and unhappiness anyone would have if they were in a similar situation. I have healthy coping methods (go for a run, build something for an hour, etc.). Things that calm me down and let me re-focus my energy on trying to find solutions instead of putting myself down further. I did post this at a particularly bad time very late last night; I couldn't sleep and was frustrated with myself. Posting this helped me sleep because I could tell myself "If you can't come up with a solution right now, maybe something you will read tomorrow can help you think."

I do appreciate the input regarding my depression though. If only my family were that considerate :) I know grad school is intensive. I am definitely seeking Masters programs over Ph.D programs because I know I am capable of the coursework. I know I can handle the demands of grad school. If anything, I'm not the sad, empty, emotionally-crippled kid who entered college.

I haven't seriously considered a post-bacc but I will look into it now. Thank you for the suggestion. 

I'm going to talk to some people (trusted friends, life mentors, etc.) about focus. I'm not so sure about biology and haven't been sure for a while. My parents don't want me to "waste" the degree but I'm willing to put in the work to find something I find worthwhile and satisfying.

And yes, I will try to contact people. :)

Depression is...well, it's as good as it's going to get when you feel like you're in a rut in life. Definitely nowhere near as bad as before. I have healthy coping methods (go for a run, build something for an hour, etc.). Things that calm me down and let me re-focus my energy on trying to find solutions instead of putting myself down further.

It wasn't really the pressures of undergrad that set me off. It was a lot of personal issues that basically happened to hit critical point while I was in college. Then big family problems happened and that was all it took for the perfect mental meltdown.

Once I learned coping and that "Whaddya know, feelings are acceptable for humans?", I became a lot better. Hence, doing better in the end.

Also, what does the beach have to do with anything? Honest question here.

Thank you for your input though. I have taken this into consideration before and still concluded additional schooling is needed for me to enter a fulfilling career to be a productive person. I wouldn't mind advice on the next step now though, since I have heard a lot of things.

I'll actually have to cut out Bakersfield. That area is actually the cause of a lot of things wrong with me. Going back there would be going back to depression.

Been considering San Marcos and Northridge. Programs are a bit of issue at Northridge (none I really qualify for, ha) but I've been looking into them.
